<reason>Side B (CON) won a high-quality clash. The decisive frame both sides eventually agreed on was "where does the child land when verification fails," and B's answer was sharper and more consistently defended: the lying fourteen-year-old gets a safe-default, unfindable account under design law, but the full adult casino with open DMs under a ban. B caught two real contradictions: (1) PRO cannot hold that platforms are unregulable on design yet perfectly regulable on age via fines, and (2) PRO progressively narrowed the motion from banning accounts to banning "algorithmic public platforms," effectively conceding B's design-regulation framing while exempting the messaging vector where contact harms actually live. A's counter that design rules degrade over time and that B's failures are "invisible" was decent and partially answered B's harmless-failure claim, but B's fines-symmetry rebuttal (a feed is visible to a regulator's own eyes; a birthday is not) blunted it. A's pressure questions were good, but B's answers (contact rules as part of design law; opt-in verification) were direct and labelled. A also had an execution cost with a clipped opening. B's rebuttal 2 was the round that assembled PRO's concessions into a coherent, damaging picture, and B's closing ("forbids noticing her") crystallized the stakes memorably.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1 ([B2.2]-[B2.5]): inverting PRO's "one number" comparison by showing age is the one invisible thing while design rules are visible on the product surface, plus the fines dilemma — platforms cannot be simultaneously unregulable on design and perfectly regulable on age. This forced A onto the defensive for the rest of the debate.</best_rebuttal>
